subsection: 6. Chemistry in society and the media

notes.b: Chemistry has been shaped by individual scientists whose discoveries changed how people live. For each one, know what they did, when, and what the impact on society was, including any downside.
points: Robert Boyle (born 25 January 1627 at Lismore Castle, Co. Waterford) pioneered experimental chemistry and argued that knowledge should come from experiment, not just from argument or authority.
Boyle's law, published in 1662, relates the pressure and volume of a gas, so it gave chemists a measured, testable rule about how gases behave.
Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table (a chart that arranges the elements in order) in 1869, and he left gaps in it for elements not yet discovered.
Mendeleev predicted the properties of those undiscovered elements, which showed the table was more than a list; the periodic table now organises all of chemistry.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic (a medicine that kills bacteria), in 1928; he shared the Nobel Prize (a major international award) in 1945 with Florey and Chain.
Penicillin was mass-produced from the 1940s, so it became widely available, and antibiotics have since saved very many lives.
Fritz Haber developed the ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen (Nobel Prize 1918), and Carl Bosch scaled it up industrially in the early 1900s, so it could be run in large factories.

Ammonia-based fertilisers (chemicals added to soil to help crops grow) help feed much of the world's population, but the same chemistry was used to make explosives: a discovery can have both positive and negative impacts.

John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino developed the lithium-ion battery (a rechargeable battery), for which they received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; it powers phones, laptops and electric vehicles.
notes.tip: If asked to describe a named scientist's contribution and its impact, give the discovery, the date, and an impact on society. Haber and Bosch let you give both a positive and a negative impact. You do not need the conditions of the Haber process here.

notes.h: The role and importance of chemistry
notes.b: Chemistry matters at three levels: to each person's daily life, to society as a whole, and to the planet. Each level has its own examples.
points: Personal: chemistry provides medicines, clean water, food, cleaning products, cosmetics, and materials for clothing and phones.
Personal: understanding chemical labels and hazards helps people make safe choices, for example when storing or using household products.
Social: chemistry supports public health through water treatment, vaccines (preparations that train the body to fight a disease) and medicines.

Social: chemistry supports agriculture through fertilisers and pesticides (chemicals that kill pests that damage crops), and provides jobs in the chemical and pharmaceutical (medicine-making) industry.
Ireland has a large pharmaceutical industry, so chemistry provides jobs here in particular.
Global: chemistry helps tackle climate change (the warming of the Earth) through cleaner fuels, batteries and carbon capture (trapping carbon dioxide before it enters the air).
Global: chemistry helps tackle pollution, food security (everyone having enough food) and the use of resources.

notes.b: Science does not happen in isolation. The society around scientists affects which questions get studied and which methods are allowed.
points: Funding: governments, companies and charities decide what research is funded, often according to social needs or profit, so money steers which problems get studied.
Public concern and urgent problems drive research, for example the search for vaccines during a pandemic (a disease outbreak spreading across the world), or for alternatives to fossil fuels.
Laws and regulations, for example on chemical safety, emissions (gases released into the air) and animal testing, limit or direct research.
The ethical values of society (its beliefs about right and wrong) decide what research is acceptable.
notes.tip: If asked for ways society influences research, pick two of these four: funding, public concern and urgent problems, laws and regulations, or ethical values. Give a short example with each.

notes.h: Economic, social, sustainability and ethical factors
notes.b: When chemistry is applied to a real issue, the science is not the only consideration. Four kinds of factor influence whether and how it is used, and people can also act on them personally.
points: Economic factors include the cost of development, production and disposal, jobs and profit, because a process that is too expensive may never be used.
Social factors include effects on health, safety, communities and quality of life.
Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising future generations, through the use of renewable resources and energy (ones that are not used up) and the management of waste.
Ethical factors include whether an application is right, for example fairness, risks to people or the environment, and informed consent (people agreeing only after being told the risks).
Being personally effective means making informed choices, for example about recycling, energy use and product claims, and taking part in public debate using evidence.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to discuss economic, social, ethical or sustainability factors in a chemical application. Name the factor and then say how it affects the application.

notes.b: The specification links all its topics through a few big ideas. These help you connect individual pieces of chemistry to the world outside the lab.
points: The specification's three cross-cutting themes are Health, Sustainability and Technology.
The themes are lenses (ways of looking) for studying how chemistry applies to real life, and the written examination includes questions on them.

notes.b: Most people meet science through news, advertising and social media rather than through the original research. That makes it important to check what they say before believing it.
points: News, advertising and social media may simplify, exaggerate or sensationalise (make more dramatic than the facts justify) science.
They may report a single study as settled fact, or leave out uncertainty and context, so a tentative result sounds like proof.
Headlines are written to attract attention, so they may not match the findings of the study.

notes.h: Questions to ask of a media claim
notes.b: A checklist of questions lets you test any claim, whether it is a news report or an advertisement. Each one looks at a different weakness a claim might have.
points: What exactly is being claimed, and is it a scientific claim, meaning one that can be tested with evidence?
Where does the claim come from: is the original study named, peer-reviewed (checked by independent experts before publication) and available to read?

How strong is the evidence: what is the sample size (how many were tested), were there controls (a comparison group), have the results been reproduced (repeated by others), and was the study done in people, animals or cells?
Is cause being confused with correlation? Two things happening together (correlation) does not prove that one causes the other.
Who benefits: is the source selling a product or promoting a view, and who funded the research?
Do other independent experts and sources agree?
Are scientific words used correctly, or misused to sound convincing, for example “chemical-free” or “natural means safe”?
notes.tip: You may be asked to evaluate a given media claim about a chemical product, or to state three questions you would ask about a report. Choose questions from this list and apply them to the claim given.

notes.b: Once a claim has been checked, you need to discuss it fairly. Good discussion keeps facts and opinions apart.
points: Separate evidence from opinion, and base conclusions on the weight of the evidence, meaning how much good evidence there is on each side.
Acknowledge uncertainty and the limits of current knowledge, because science can say what the evidence shows so far but cannot always give a final answer.
Consider different perspectives, economic, social, ethical and environmental, while keeping the scientific evidence separate from them.

notes.h: Common misleading claims and the chemistry
notes.b: Some claims appear again and again in advertising and online. Each can be answered with a fact from chemistry.
points: “Chemical-free”: everything, including water and food, is made of chemicals, so nothing can truly be chemical-free.
“Natural is always safe; synthetic (man-made) is dangerous”: toxicity (how poisonous something is) depends on the substance and the dose, not on whether it is natural.
Some natural substances are highly toxic, and a synthetic substance can be identical to a natural one, so the origin does not change the chemistry.
Alkaline-water and detox claims: the body controls its own pH (the scale that measures how acidic or alkaline a liquid is), and drinking alkaline water does not change blood pH.
Human blood pH is kept between about 7.35 and 7.45.
Stomach acid has a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5, so it is strongly acidic and would quickly neutralise any alkaline water swallowed.
notes.tip: You may be asked to evaluate a claim such as a product being chemical-free and natural, so completely safe. Use the chemical-free point and the natural-versus-synthetic point, and ask where the claim comes from and who benefits. Do not name real newspapers, companies or products.

questions.prompt: Describe the contribution of one named scientist to chemistry and evaluate its impact on society.
questions.model: Fritz Haber developed the ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen, for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1918, and Carl Bosch scaled the process up industrially. Ammonia is used to make fertilisers that help feed much of the world's population, a positive impact on food security. The same chemistry was used to make explosives, a negative impact. The overall impact therefore depends on how the discovery is used, and it raises ethical and economic questions for society.

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which society influences scientific research.
questions.model: Funding: governments, companies and charities decide which research is funded, often according to social needs or profit. Public concern and urgent problems drive research, e.g. the search for vaccines during a pandemic.

questions.prompt: An advertisement claims a shampoo is 'chemical-free and 100% natural, so it is completely safe'. Evaluate this claim.
questions.model: The claim that the shampoo is chemical-free is misleading, because everything, including water, is made of chemicals. The claim that it is natural and therefore safe is also misleading, because toxicity depends on the substance and the dose, not on whether it is natural; some natural substances are highly toxic. The source should be checked: the advertisement is selling the product, so its claims may present only one side, and it should be asked whether the safety claim is supported by a named, peer-reviewed study. Other independent sources should be checked to see whether they agree that the product is completely safe.

questions.prompt: State three questions you would ask to evaluate a newspaper report of a new scientific discovery.
questions.model: Three questions: What exactly is being claimed, and is it testable with evidence? Is the original study named, peer-reviewed and available, and how strong is its evidence, including its sample size, controls and whether the results have been reproduced? Who benefits from the claim, and who funded the research? Other questions include whether cause is being confused with correlation, and whether independent experts agree.
